case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Elections Clause (Article I, Section 4) of the U.S. Constitution grants state legislatures exclusive and plenary authority to regulate federal elections, precluding state courts from reviewing such regulations under state constitutional provisions.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Article I, Section 4 (Elections Clause) of the U.S. Constitution.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Article I, Section 4 delegates exclusive authority to state legislatures to set the "Times, Places and Manner" of federal elections. They contend that the North Carolina Supreme Court usurped this federal grant of authority by striking down a congressional districting map based on state constitutional provisions, thereby violating the independent state legislature doctrine. They view the regulation of congressional elections as a "federal function" limited only by the Federal Constitution.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that state courts have the authority to review state legislative actions concerning federal elections, including redistricting, under state constitutional provisions. They cite precedents like *Rucho v. Common Cause* and *Arizona State Legislature v. Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission* to support the role of state courts in applying state law to guard against issues like partisan gerrymandering. They also raise procedural arguments, asserting that the case is not ripe for review as it involves interlocutory decisions and that petitioners' arguments were not properly presented at the trial court. They reject the notion that election regulation is solely a "federal function" as argued by petitioners, citing *Smiley v. Holm*.
